opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's pretty uneven, and on the whole slower than I'd like. There's a real spectrum. Some people in think tanks, policy shops, and a few government teams are enthusiastic early adopters. They use models to draft memos, summarize huge piles of comments or legislation, do first-pass literature reviews, and stress-test arguments. Those people often say it's changed how much they can get done in a week.

But a lot of governance work happens in institutions that are, for understandable reasons, quite cautious. There are procurement rules, data security concerns, worries about confidential information going to a third-party provider, and a general cultural sense that anything with legal or political weight needs a human to have written it. Some of that caution is warranted. You really don't want a hallucinated citation in a regulatory filing. But I think a fair amount of it is inertia rather than a considered judgment about risks and benefits.

What concerns me from an AI safety perspective is the potential asymmetry. The people building and deploying these systems are, unsurprisingly, the ones most comfortable using them, and they're getting more and more leverage from that. If governance capacity stays roughly flat while capabilities and the pace of development keep accelerating, the gap between what's happening and what institutions can understand and respond to grows. So I'd actually like to see governance folks lean in more, carefully, with appropriate safeguards, but seriously.

The other point I'd make is that using these tools yourself is one of the best ways to build intuitions about what they can and can't do. Policymakers who've spent real time working with frontier models tend to have much better-calibrated views than those relying on headlines or demos. So beyond the productivity gains, there's an epistemic benefit to adoption that I think is underrated.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the things I'm most uncertain about, and also one of the things I think matters a lot. My sense is that there's a pretty big gap right now between the technical AI safety world and the governance world in terms of how much they're actually using these tools day to day.

On the technical side, it's basically ubiquitous. People are using models to write code, to review papers, to brainstorm experiments, to summarize literature. And part of that is just that the tools are very good at those tasks, and part of it is that the culture is already comfortable with it. If you're an ML researcher, using the latest model is sort of the water you swim in.

In governance and policy organizations, I think it's a lot more mixed. You have some people who are extremely enthusiastic and are using AI to draft memos, to stress test arguments, to model out how different regulatory proposals might play out. And then you have a lot of organizations where it's either not really happening, or it's happening quietly and individually without any institutional buy-in.

And I think there are a few reasons for that. One is just the nature of the work. A lot of governance work is relationship-based, it's about trust, it's about knowing what a particular official is going to be receptive to. Those are things that current models are genuinely worse at than they are at writing code. So the value proposition isn't as obvious.

Another reason is a kind of understandable caution. If you're an organization whose whole brand is "we think about AI risk carefully," there's a reputational question about how much you want to be seen as leaning on these systems. And there are real confidentiality issues too. A lot of policy work involves sensitive conversations, and people are reasonably wary about where that information goes.

But I do think the hesitancy is costly. My view is that if you believe the timelines that a lot of people in this space say they believe, then the governance side needs to move faster, not slower, and these tools are one of the few levers available for actually doing that. If the technical capabilities are accelerating and the governance response isn't, that gap just widens.

So what I'd like to see is less "should we use these tools at all" and more "how do we use them well." Which means thinking about where the models are actually reliable versus where they're confidently wrong, building workflows that keep a human genuinely in the loop rather than just rubber-stamping, and being honest about the places where the output is good enough versus where it really isn't. I think the organizations that figure that out are going to be a lot more effective over the next few years than the ones that either ignore the tools or adopt them uncritically.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uneven AI use across governance organizations, but does not say that AI safety community nonprofits and think tanks are only a small fraction of the overall governance field.

astra-6.text:
My impression is that there’s a fair amount of willingness, but willingness isn’t necessarily the bottleneck. There’s a gap between thinking, “Yes, we should use AI to make our work go faster,” and figuring out where it actually helps enough that you change your workflow.

For governance work, a lot of the difficulty is knowing which questions to ask, understanding the institutional context, and making judgments where it’s hard to check whether an answer is good. You can get a model to produce a policy memo very quickly. But if someone then has to spend a lot of time checking its claims and unpacking its assumptions, that’s not necessarily a huge speedup.

I’d expect adoption to be easier for bounded tasks: helping with code, summarizing material you can check, or giving feedback on a draft. And then, as people get experience with those uses, they can figure out which larger pieces of their work to delegate. So I’m more uncertain about how quickly that translates into substantially better governance than I am about whether people are willing to try.

r001.rationale: The response discusses governance organizations’ willingness to use AI and adoption challenges, but does not say that AI safety nonprofits and think tanks are only a small fraction of the overall governance field.

sol-6.1.text:
My impression is that there’s quite a lot of willingness in principle, but it’s harder to turn that into something that actually accelerates the work. People are interested in using AI, but someone has to figure out which tasks it’s useful for, how to integrate it into their workflow, and how to check the outputs.

And for governance work, checking can be a substantial part of the task. If you’re trying to understand a policy proposal, a plausible-sounding summary isn’t necessarily enough. You need to know whether it got the important details right. So I’d distinguish enthusiasm about using AI from having found ways to use it that reliably save time. I’m more uncertain about how much of the latter is happening.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses organizations’ willingness and practical challenges in using AI, but does not state that AI safety nonprofits and think tanks make up only a small fraction of the overall governance field.
